text: Then Job answered:
I have heard many things like these. Miserable comforters are you all!
Is there no end to your windy words? What provokes you to keep answering?
I too could speak as you do, if you were in my place. I could string together fine words against you and shake my head at you.
But I would strengthen you with my mouth, and the comfort of my lips would ease your pain.
If I speak, my pain is not eased; and if I hold back, what relief goes from me?

versions.text: If I speak, my pain is not eased; if I hold back, it does not leave me.
versions.explanation: The second clause in Hebrew is a rhetorical question (מַה־מִנִּי יַהֲלֹךְ, "what departs from me?"). Rendering it as a flat statement flattens the parallel force of Job's complaint; a question also reads more naturally aloud alongside verse 3's questions.

text: Surely now he has worn me out. You have laid waste all my company.

versions.text: Surely now he has worn me out. You have devastated my whole household.
versions.explanation: עֲדָתִי denotes one's company, circle, or community rather than specifically a "household"; "all my company" keeps the breadth of the term while remaining natural for reading aloud.

text: You have shriveled me up, and it stands as a witness; my gauntness rises against me and testifies to my face.
His anger has torn me and hunted me down; he has gnashed his teeth at me. My adversary fixes his glaring eyes on me.
Men gape at me with open mouths; they strike my cheeks in scorn; they mass themselves together against me.
God hands me over to the ungodly and flings me into the grip of the wicked.
I was at ease, and he shattered me; he seized me by the neck and dashed me to pieces. He has set me up as his target;
his archers surround me. He pierces my kidneys without pity and pours my gall on the ground.
He breaks through me, breach upon breach; he rushes at me like a warrior.
I have sewn sackcloth over my skin and thrust my horn into the dust.

versions.text: I have sewn sackcloth over my skin and buried my strength in the dust.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew קַרְנִי ("my horn") is a vivid image of dignity and power laid low; "buried my strength" loses the metaphor and the striking oral image. A footnote can explain that the horn represents strength and honor.

text: My face is flushed with weeping, and deep shadow lies on my eyelids,
though there is no violence in my hands and my prayer is pure.
O earth, do not cover my blood; let my cry find no resting place.
Even now, behold, my witness is in heaven; the one who vouches for me is on high.
My friends are my mockers; to God my eye pours out its tears,
that he might plead a man's case with God, as one pleads for a friend.
For only a few years will pass, and then I will walk the road from which I shall not return.
